questions.question: State one reason why the exchange of biological material across borders needs to be regulated. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Role in Branding
  • • Identity and recognition: A trademark gives a unique identity to a product or company,
  • helping consumers easily recognize it among competitors.
  • • Brand loyalty: When customers trust a brand’s quality, its trademark helps build loyalty
  • and repeat purchases.
  • • Marketing tool: Trademarks make advertising more effective, as logos, names, or symbols
  • attract attention and convey brand values.
  • • Business reputation: A strong trademark reflects a company’s reputation and goodwill in
  • the market.
  • • Competitive advantage: Trademarks legally protect brand elements, preventing others
  • from copying or imitating them.

• Role in Consumer Protection

questions.question: Define informed consent. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Ethical Concerns in Organ Transplantation
  • • Organ trade and exploitation: Poor people may be exploited for their organs due to
  • financial need.
  • • Fair distribution: Ethical issues arise over how organs are allocated —who gets priority
  • and why.
  • • Consent and autonomy: Organs should only be taken with proper consent from donors or
  • their families.
  • • Cultural and religious beliefs: Some traditions may object to organ removal after death.
  • • Use of animal or artificial organs: Raises questions about crossing species boundaries and
  • long-term safety.

questions.question: Explain the concept of novelty in patenting biotech inventions. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the concept of novelty in patenting biotech inventions. [U] / [CO1]
  • The invention must be new and not previously known or disclosed anywhere in the world
  • before the patent application is filed. The concept of novelty is one of the key requirements
  • for granting a patent in biotechnology and other fields. It ensures tha t only truly new and
  • original inventions receive protection. In biotechnology, novelty means that the invention —
  • such as a new gene sequence, microorganism, genetically modified plant, or process— has not
  • been made public anywhere in the world before the date of the patent application.

questions.question: Define trademark infringement and explain its essential features. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Define trademark infringement and explain its essential features. [U] / [CO5]
  • Trademark infringement is the unauthorized use of a registered trademark or a deceptively similar
  • mark by another party, in a way that is likely to cause confusion, deception, or misunderstanding
  • among consumers about the origin of goods or services.
  • • Unauthorized use: The trademark is used without the permission of the registered owner.
  • • Identical or deceptively similar mark: The infringing mark closely resembles the registered
  • one in appearance, sound, or meaning.
